import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

A client that holds an account root and a device key, and runs no node of its own,
reaches a context through somebody else's node. This page is the contract for that:
the exact bytes it signs, the exact shapes it sends, and which parts are live today.

It exists so a client can be built against a fixed target rather than against a
guess. Every field here is quoted from the code that implements it, and anything
still due to change says so where it appears.

<Aside type="caution" title="Read the status markers">
**Live** means implemented and callable on a node today. Every exchange on this
page is now live; the one thing still moving is the warrant's field set, and it is
marked where it appears rather than left for you to discover from a verification
failure.
</Aside>

| Contract | Status | Tracking |
|---|---|---|
| Discovery — where to write and as whom | **Live** | — |
| Warrant and delegated write | **Live** (field set changes) | [#3933](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/issues/3933) |
| Session — challenge and `LoginStatement` | **Live** | [#3930](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/issues/3930) |
| Read — an authenticated account reads a context | **Live** | [#3931](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/issues/3931) |

## 0. Primitives

Two conventions run through everything below.

### Domain-separated hashing

Every signature in Calimero is over a 32-byte digest produced by one function, so
a signature minted for one purpose can never be replayed as another. Length-prefixing
each segment is what stops `("ab", "c")` and `("a", "bc")` hashing alike.

```rust
// crates/primitives/src/identity.rs
pub fn domain_hash(domain: &[u8], parts: &[&[u8]]) -> [u8; 32] {
    let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
    hasher.update((domain.len() as u64).to_le_bytes());
    hasher.update(domain);
    for part in parts {
        hasher.update((part.len() as u64).to_le_bytes());
        hasher.update(part);
    }
    hasher.finalize().into()
}
```

In other words: `SHA256( u64le(len(domain)) ‖ domain ‖ ( u64le(len(part)) ‖ part )* )`,
with every length a little-endian `u64`.

A client implementing this in another language must reproduce it byte for byte.
It is the single most likely place for a cross-language client to go wrong, because
a missing length prefix still produces plausible-looking digests that never verify.

### Encoding on the wire

Signed structures cross the HTTP boundary as **hex-encoded borsh**, never as JSON.
The canonical form of a signed statement is its borsh encoding; re-describing its
fields as JSON would create a second spelling that could disagree with the bytes
the signature covers.

Everything unsigned — request envelopes, arguments, responses — is JSON, camelCase.

## 1. Discovery — live today

Before minting a warrant a client needs two facts it cannot derive: which node to
talk to, and which account that node will name as `executor`.

**Which relay**, from the cloud:

```http
GET /api/cloud/me/namespaces/{namespace_id}/relays
```

```jsonc
{
  "namespace_id": "…",
  "relays": [
    {
      "peer_id": "12D3KooW…",
      "relay_url": "https://node-7.example.net",   // where to send the intent
      "executor_account": "…",                      // what the warrant must name
      "authorship_ready": true,                     // may it author here yet
      "status": "active",
      "assigned_at": "…", "confirmed_at": "…", "last_seen_at": "…"
    }
  ]
}
```

**Whether this context is open to delegation**, from the node itself:

```http
GET /admin-api/contexts/{context_id}/intents
```

```jsonc
{
  "executorAccount": "…",
  "canAuthorOnBehalf": false,
  "groupId": "…",
  "grantedOnGroupId": null
}
```

`canAuthorOnBehalf: false` is the **default state of every context** — authorship is
implied by neither membership nor admin, and is never granted implicitly. A client
should read this before signing anything and, when it is false, tell the user to ask
an admin of `groupId` for the grant rather than minting a warrant that will be
refused after the nonce is already spent.

## 2. Warrant and delegated write

### What a warrant commits to

```rust
// crates/account/src/warrant.rs — live today
pub struct Warrant {
    pub context: ContextId,
    pub author_account: AccountId,
    pub author_device_key: PublicKey,
    pub executor: AccountId,
    pub intent_hash: [u8; 32],
    pub nonce: u64,
    pub not_after: u64,
    pub signature: [u8; 64],
}
```

The intent is committed to as a hash, not carried in the clear:

```rust
intent_hash = domain_hash(b"calimero.warrant.intent.v1", &[method.as_bytes(), args])
```

And the signature covers, in this order:

```rust
signature = sign(domain_hash(b"calimero.warrant.v1", &[
    context.digest(),
    author_account.as_bytes(),
    author_device_key,              // 32 bytes
    executor.as_bytes(),
    intent_hash,                    // 32 bytes
    &nonce.to_le_bytes(),
    &not_after.to_le_bytes(),
]))
```

### The field set is changing

[#3933](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/issues/3933) adds `method` in the clear
(so peers can select a per-method write-set), `app_version`, and cited `account_heads` /
`governance_floor`, and may replace `not_after` with a governance height. **Every one of
those changes the signed bytes**, and the signing domain bumps to `calimero.warrant.v2`.

There is no backwards compatibility: warrants signed under `v1` will stop verifying.
Build the builder so the field list and the domain constant are in one place.

<Aside type="note" title="Why not_after is not checked at apply">
`not_after` is a wall clock, and a wall clock must never gate an apply. Peers apply at
different times, so a warrant that expired between two receivers would be accepted by
one and refused by the other, and authorization would stop converging. The bound is
checked by the relay at the API boundary, where one clock decides and nothing has
converged yet.
</Aside>

### Submitting it

```http
POST /admin-api/contexts/{context_id}/intents
```

```jsonc
{
  "method": "set",
  "argsJson": { "key": "a", "value": "b" },
  "warrant":     "<hex borsh of Warrant>",
  "authorProof": "<hex borsh of AccountProof<DeviceCert>>"
}
```

The client supplies only **its own half** of the proof. The executor's proof and
signing key are attached by the node from its own credentials, because the warrant
authorizes an operator *account* and the author has no business knowing which of
that operator's processes will run it.

```jsonc
// 200
{
  "data": {
    "rootHash": "…",              // the context's scope root after the run
    "returns":  { /* the method's own return value, or null */ }
  }
}
```

`AccountProof<T>` is the self-contained credential that ties a device key to an account:

```rust
// crates/account/src/signed.rs
pub struct AccountProof<T> {
    pub genesis: AccountGenesis,        // hashes to the AccountId
    pub chain: Vec<RootKeyHandoff>,     // root rollovers, epoch 0 upward
    pub statement: T,                   // here: DeviceCert
}
```

## 3. Session — live

A device key obtains a session in two calls. Implemented by
[#3930](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/issues/3930); enable the
`account_proof` provider on the node to use it.

### Challenge

```http
GET /auth/challenge
```

```jsonc
{
  "data": {
    "challenge": "<64 hex chars — 32 bytes>",
    "expires_at": 1789470000          // unix seconds; 60s from issue by default
  },
  "error": null
}
```

The 32 bytes are `expiry(8) ‖ nonce(8) ‖ tag(16)`, the tag an HMAC over the first two
under a key only the node holds. So the node stores nothing at issue time — which
matters, because this endpoint is unauthenticated and a per-request row would hand
an anonymous caller a write amplifier.

It is single-use, and **spent only after a signature over it verifies**. Burning it
on presentation would let anyone who can see a challenge in flight invalidate it
before its holder finishes signing.

`404` means the provider is not enabled on this node.

### LoginStatement

```rust
// domain calimero.auth.login.v1 · borsh · signed by the DEVICE key
// crates/account/src/login.rs
pub struct LoginStatement {
    pub node: PublicKey,             // this node's identity, as the client pinned it
    pub audience: Audience,          // WebOrigin(String) | CodeSigningId(String) | Cli
    pub challenge: [u8; 32],
    pub session_key: PublicKey,      // the ephemeral key the session speaks with
    pub device_key: PublicKey,       // what the signature is checked against
    pub issued_at: u64,
    pub expires_at: u64,
    pub signature: [u8; 64],
}
```

```rust
signature = sign(domain_hash(b"calimero.auth.login.v1", &[
    node,                            // 32 bytes
    &audience_tag_and_bytes,         // 1-byte variant tag, then the payload
    &challenge,                      // 32 bytes
    session_key,                     // 32 bytes
    device_key,                      // 32 bytes
    &issued_at.to_le_bytes(),
    &expires_at.to_le_bytes(),
]))
```

The audience tag is `0` for `WebOrigin`, `1` for `CodeSigningId`, `2` for `Cli`,
followed by the variant's string bytes (empty for `Cli`). The tag is load-bearing:
without it a statement minted for the web origin `"x"` would verify as one minted
for the code-signing id `"x"`.

The client learns the node's identity from a pinned certificate, **never from the
challenge** — otherwise an attacker who can answer on the node's behalf chooses what
the device signs about. That is the field's whole purpose: a hostile relay can fetch
a real challenge from the target node and serve it to a user as its own, and only
`node` refuses the replay.

### Exchange

The login goes through the node's existing token endpoint, with
`auth_method: "account_proof"` — not a bespoke route. That is what gives a
device-key session the same refresh, revocation and rate limiting every other
session gets.

```http
POST /auth/token
```

```jsonc
{
  "auth_method": "account_proof",
  "public_key":  "<the session public key — must match the statement's session_key>",
  "client_name": "<the node URL, for node-binding the token>",
  "timestamp":   1789470000,
  "provider_data": {
    "challenge":       "<64 hex chars>",
    "login_statement": "<hex borsh of LoginStatement>",
    "account_proof":   "<hex borsh of AccountProof<DeviceCert>>"
  }
}
```

```jsonc
// 200
{
  "data": {
    "access_token":  "<JWT; subject is the ACCOUNT, not the device>",
    "refresh_token": "<JWT>"
  },
  "error": null
}
```

The session is granted to the **account**: the JWT's `sub` is the account id, which
`/auth/validate` forwards to handlers as `X-Auth-User`.

Membership is *not* established by logging in. It is evaluated per request against
the target context's group — a relay serves several tenants, so a session must not
carry a standing right to read.

<Aside type="caution" title="What a session grants today">
By default a session from this provider carries `context:intent` **and nothing
else** — the delegated-write path, which is already gated by the warrant and by
`CAN_AUTHOR_ON_BEHALF`, so the session adds no authority the warrant did not already
prove. Reads are deliberately excluded until the per-request membership check lands
with [#3931](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/issues/3931); without it a
broader default would let any account with a device key read every context on a
shared relay. Operators widen it with `auth.account_proof.session_permissions`.
</Aside>

<Aside type="danger" title="A session is not a warrant">
A session authenticates the caller **to this relay**. It never substitutes for a
warrant on a write: a warrant proves to peers who never saw the HTTP request that the
author consented to that operation, and a bearer token scoped to one relay cannot do
that. Reads need no warrant, because a read publishes nothing and so has no peer to
convince.
</Aside>

## 4. Read — live

Implemented by [#3931](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/issues/3931).

```http
POST /admin-api/contexts/{context_id}/query
Authorization: Bearer <session token>
```

```jsonc
{
  "method": "get",
  "argsJson": { "key": "a" }
}
```

```jsonc
// 200
{ "data": { "returns": { /* the method's return value */ } } }
```

Three refusals a client must handle distinctly, because they mean different things
to a user:

| Status | Meaning | What the client should do |
|---|---|---|
| `401` | no session, or it expired | re-run the login exchange |
| `403` | the account is not a member of this context's group | tell the user; do not retry |
| `409` | the method is not read-only | a bug in the client's method choice — this is a write, mint a warrant |

That last one is the one to get right. Reads are gated on the method being declared
read-only, and the gate **fails closed**: a method that declares nothing is refused
rather than guessed at. See [#3932](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/issues/3932)
for how that declaration is derived from the method's receiver — which is why the
gate is usable at all, and why a client can call an ordinary `&self` method without
the app author having annotated anything.

Three things about this endpoint are worth knowing before building against it.

**The account is never in the body.** It comes from the session, so there is no
field a caller could set to read as somebody else. A session that is not
account-anchored — a node-owner or client-key token — gets `401` here, not because
it lacks permission but because this route answers "what may *this account* see"
and such a session names no account. A node owner reads through the ordinary
execute path.

**Membership is re-checked on every call**, against the group owning the context,
never cached from the session. One relay serves several tenants, so a session that
carried a standing right to read would keep serving somebody after the removal op
the node has already applied. Inheritance resolves, so a subgroup member reads a
context they hold through a parent.

**No `rootHash` in the response**, unlike the intent reply. That field answers "did
this change anything?" and for a read the answer is structurally no; returning it
would invite a client to watch it for changes that can never come.

<Aside type="note" title="Token scope">
The read route is gated on `context:query[<context_id>]`, its own permission —
not `context:execute` (which also covers join, leave and resync) and not
`context:intent` (which submits writes). A session minted by the `account_proof`
provider carries `context:intent` and `context:query` and nothing else, which is
the delegated client's whole surface. Both are gated again below the token: a
write by the warrant and `CAN_AUTHOR_ON_BEHALF`, a read by the per-call membership
check above. The token decides who may **ask**.
</Aside>

## 5. End to end

```
1.  GET  /api/cloud/me/namespaces/{ns}/relays      → relay_url, executor_account
2.  GET  /auth/challenge                           → challenge
3.  sign LoginStatement with the DEVICE key
4.  POST /auth/token  (auth_method=account_proof)  → session token
5.  GET  /admin-api/contexts/{ctx}/intents         → canAuthorOnBehalf?
    ├── false → stop; ask an admin of groupId for the grant
    └── true  → continue
6.  READ   POST /admin-api/contexts/{ctx}/query    (token; no warrant)
7.  WRITE  sign a Warrant with the DEVICE key
           POST /admin-api/contexts/{ctx}/intents  (token + warrant + authorProof)
```

Every step works today.

## Test vectors

Check your implementation against these before pointing it at a node. They are
asserted by the Rust tests named beside each block, so they cannot drift from the
code without CI going red.

### `domain_hash`

`crates/account/src/tests/domain.rs::domain_hash_has_known_answers`

| domain | parts | digest |
|---|---|---|
| `""` | — | `af5570f5a1810b7af78caf4bc70a660f0df51e42baf91d4de5b2328de0e83dfc` |
| `"ab"` | `["c"]` | `43ee655579de01ca739b3f95c1c2d3f46d353b2c0df818064ea594506cdb2617` |
| `"a"` | `["bc"]` | `9a8acca1b6c6c0befd3fbc756aed625da998c998f7252e738c4ef061906b9b21` |

Start with the first row. It is SHA-256 of **eight zero bytes** — the `u64le`
length of an empty domain — not SHA-256 of the empty string. If you get
`e3b0c442…`, you are omitting the length prefixes, and nothing below will match.

The last two rows are the whole reason the prefixes exist: both hash the letters
`abc`, and they must differ.

### Warrant

`crates/account/src/tests/warrant_wire_fixture.rs`

Inputs: `context` = `0x11`×32, `author_account` = `0x22`×32, `executor` =
`0x33`×32, `method` = `"set"`, `args` = `{"key":"k","value":"v"}` (exactly those
bytes, no whitespace), `nonce` = 42, `not_after` = 1700000000, author device
secret = `0x07` seeded.

```text
intent_hash       dc066cc8524c74dc21714174009df536376e3151f5b92f0a676defde599dbae5
signing preimage  a5d5f7aa368f8d79edd0667f60c41239a7dedaf8765e4e72ef3031bbacd15f35
author_device_key ea4a6c63e29c520abef5507b132ec5f9954776aebebe7b92421eea691446d22c
```

The full 240-byte encoding, field by field — pure concatenation, every field
fixed-width, no borsh length prefixes or tags, which is what makes a non-borsh
implementation viable:

```text
offset  field              bytes  value
     0  context               32  1111…11
    32  author_account        32  2222…22
    64  author_device_key     32  ea4a6c63…
    96  executor              32  3333…33
   128  intent_hash           32  dc066cc8…
   160  nonce                  8  2a00000000000000   (42, little-endian)
   168  not_after              8  00f1536500000000   (1700000000, little-endian)
   176  signature             64  a3ddd529…
```

Both `u64`s are **little-endian**, here and in `domain_hash`. That is the second
most common cross-language mistake after the missing length prefix, and it
produces a warrant that is well-formed and verifies nowhere.

<Aside type="note" title="No stub to run">
There is no mock server for sections 3 and 4. A stub that verifies shapes but not
signatures teaches a client that a wrong signature is acceptable — exactly the
error a real node exists to catch, and the one that is most expensive to discover
late. The vectors above pin the half of the contract a client can get wrong on its
own; the rest is worth testing against a real node.
</Aside>
